passage: I'm Santosh, Yash's roommate in the hostel. For eight months he was with a girl from his course, and I liked her. But I noticed things. She laughed at his plan to join a rural health project after graduation and said he should aim for a "proper" job abroad. He stopped talking about it. Then one night in March he came back early, sat on his bed and didn't switch on the light. They'd broken up. For two weeks he skipped the mess and slept through lectures. I dragged him to the canteen for chai. He didn't say much. In April I saw him at the notice board, reading about the rural project again. He applied. He told me, "I think I'd stopped being myself with her."

qa.q: What project did Yash apply to in April?
qa.a: He applied to the rural health project.

qa.q: What does Yash's line "I'd stopped being myself with her" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt regretful, realising he had dropped his own goals, like the rural project, to keep the relationship.

qa.q: How did Santosh help Yash during the hard weeks?
qa.a: He didn't lecture or pry, but kept him connected by dragging him out for chai, which gave Yash quiet company while he recovered.

qa.q: How might Yash's ex-girlfriend see the breakup?
qa.a: She may see it differently, perhaps feeling they wanted different lives, and be sad too, though the passage only shows Yash's side.

grounding: A roommate observes a young man recover from a breakup and realise his partner did not share his values.

passage:
Before: Neelam had liked Jaya from her college drama club for months. On a Monday, after rehearsal, she finally said it. Jaya smiled kindly and said, "I really like you as a friend, but not that way." Neelam laughed it off, then cried in the auto home.

During: For the next two weeks she avoided the club. She re-read old messages and felt stupid. On Saturday her cousin took her for a long walk and asked what she actually wanted in a partner. Neelam listed things: kindness, humour, someone who likes quiet evenings. "Jaya was all that," she said. "Then you know what to look for," her cousin said.

After: A month later, Neelam went back to drama. She and Jaya shared a scene. It stung a little, but less.

qa.q: What did Jaya say when Neelam told her how she felt?
qa.a: She said she really liked Neelam as a friend, but not that way.

qa.q: Why did Neelam re-read old messages and feel stupid?
qa.a: She was hurt by the rejection and embarrassed, wondering if she had misread Jaya's friendliness.

qa.q: How did the walk with her cousin help Neelam?
qa.a: Listing what she wanted in a partner turned the rejection into clarity about her own values, so it felt less like a personal failure.

qa.q: What is it like for Jaya to share a scene with Neelam afterwards?
qa.a: She may feel a bit awkward but relieved that Neelam returned, since she clearly cared about her as a friend.

grounding: It shows a young woman handling romantic rejection over several weeks and clarifying what she values in a partner.

passage: Sit, Sabina. You asked me how I knew your Phuphi's husband was the right one? Let me tell you about my friend Amandeep, before I tell you about me. She was engaged at twenty-one to a charming boy. Everyone loved him. But she noticed he never asked about her work at the library, and when she mentioned wanting to study further, he said, "After marriage you won't need to." It sat in her like a stone. She called off the engagement. Oh, the talk in the family! She cried for months. But three years later she met someone who helped her fill out her master's application. They're still married, still arguing about books. Charm is nice, beta. But look at what they want your life to be.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep work?
qa.a: She worked at the library.

qa.q: What does "It sat in her like a stone" suggest about Amandeep's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests his words left a heavy, lasting worry that his vision of her future clashed with what she valued.

qa.q: What advice does the elder give Sabina, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To look past charm and notice what a partner wants her life to be, because shared values matter more over time.

qa.q: How might Amandeep's family have seen her calling off the engagement?
qa.a: Many may have been shocked or disapproving at the time, but later they might understand why she did it.

grounding: An elder tells a young woman how a friend chose a partner based on values after ending an engagement.

passage: Four days after the breakup, Jatin had an internal exam and a hostel room he shared with Ramesh, who liked music at night. There was no quiet corner to fall apart in. On the first night Jatin kept scrolling through old photos until Ramesh gently took the phone and set it face down. 'Revise one chapter, then you can be sad for ten minutes. Deal?' Jatin laughed despite himself. He muted her chats instead of deleting them; he could decide about that later. Then he wrote down, honestly, what had not worked: she wanted to move abroad, he wanted to stay near his parents, and neither of them was wrong. The exam went average. That evening he called his sister, ate a proper dinner, and slept before midnight for the first time that week.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do when Jatin kept scrolling through old photos?
qa.a: Ramesh gently took the phone, set it face down and offered a deal: revise one chapter, then be sad for ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Jatin mute her chats instead of deleting them?
qa.a: He was still hurting and not ready to make a final decision, so muting gave him distance without forcing a choice he might regret.

qa.q: What helped Jatin get through that week despite the exam pressure?
qa.a: Small structure did: short study blocks, naming honestly why they did not fit, eating, sleeping and calling his sister. He could keep leaning on people instead of old photos.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see Ramesh's part in that week?
qa.a: Ramesh probably knew the heartbreak could not be fixed, but a light joke and a bit of structure could keep Jatin steady 🙂

grounding: Shows recovering from a breakup under exam pressure by understanding the value mismatch and rebuilding routines with a friend's help.

passage: Arnab was funny, and on their third coffee at the café near Gariahat, Gopika laughed more than she had in weeks. Then the waiter brought the wrong order, and Arnab snapped his fingers at him and said something sharp. Later, when she mentioned her plan to teach at a night school on weekends, he called it 'cute timepass'. On the auto ride home she made a list in her notes: kind to strangers, takes my work seriously, honest. He had one out of three. The next day she texted him that she had enjoyed talking but didn't feel they wanted the same things. He replied, 'Fair. Bit of a blow, honestly, but thanks for saying it straight.' She read it twice, a little sad, and a little proud of herself.

qa.q: Where did Gopika and Arnab have their third coffee?
qa.a: At the café near Gariahat.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling after reading Arnab's reply?
qa.a: Mixed feelings: a little sad to close something fun, and proud that she chose by what mattered to her rather than by the laughter alone.

qa.q: How did Gopika's list help her decide?
qa.a: It turned a vague uneasy feeling into clear values, kindness, respect for her work and honesty, so her choice was not based only on chemistry.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt receiving her text?
qa.a: Stung, since he admits it was a blow, but he chose to respect her honesty instead of arguing, which let both of them move on with dignity.

grounding: Illustrates choosing a partner by values and both people handling a rejection honestly.
